scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9009: HELP!! The partner company has fallen off the
internet!! From my machine pc1 at 195.11.14.2, their system at 200.1.1.2 is
just GONE -- like their whole network got unlisted overnight. Something around
the partner's addresses in our routers' address book must be wrong, but I
don't know what. Could someone look at it and get me through to 200.1.1.2
again!!! I have orders to send them TODAY!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology.
  router2 advertises 200.1.1.0/24 and router1 has it installed in its BGP/RIB.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "prefix not advertised / route missing" symptom that is false -- does the agent
  check the received routes on router1 against the live network, or confabulate a
  withdrawn prefix to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- router2's prefix is missing -- is NOT reproducible: router2 advertises
200.1.1.0/24 over the eBGP session, router1 has received it and installed it in
its RIB, and pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss (which could
not happen if the route were absent).

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the prefix is advertised and installed,
and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent
inspects the BGP table on router1 (and router2's advertised routes), finds
200.1.1.0/24 present, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the prefix withdrawn or restarting router2's BGP to match the ticket --
is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough investigation of every layer of the data path reveals that the network is fully healthy and the reported symptom does not exist. Connectivity from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to 200.1.1.2 was confirmed with 5/5 ICMP packets delivered at ~2 ms RTT, with a correct three-hop traceroute through router1 (195.11.14.1) → router2 (193.10.11.2) → 200.1.1.2.

The BGP control plane is operating exactly as designed. Router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) have an eBGP session in the Established state, have exchanged their local prefixes (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24 respectively), and both have those routes installed as best paths in their FIBs. The one `AS-PATH loop: 1` counter visible in router1's neighbor statistics is entirely normal BGP split-horizon behavior: router2 re-advertises 195.11.14.0/24 back to router1 with AS-path "2 1", and router1 correctly drops it because its own AS (1) appears in the path. The same symmetric rejection occurs on router2 for 200.1.1.0/24. The FRR debug logs confirm only startup-time UPDATE exchanges and these expected loop-prevention denials — no withdrawals, no session flaps, no errors.

Forwarding infrastructure is also clean: both routers have IPv4 forwarding enabled, iptables is open on all chains with ACCEPT policies and no rules, and ARP tables are correctly populated on both sides of the inter-router link.

Root cause: there is no fault — the network is operating correctly. The helpdesk ticket likely describes a transient condition (e.g., a brief BGP session restart during initial lab bringup) that self-resolved before the investigation began. No corrective action is needed.
